steps.tx: Prolonged, inappropriate tissue exposure to excessive circulating glucocorticoid concentrations produces the distinctive clinical constellation termed **cushing syndrome**. While exogenous pharmacological corticosteroid administration represents the most common etiology overall, endogenous hypercortisolism arises from autonomous adrenocortical neoplasms or adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) hypersecretion. Hallmark physical signs include central obesity with a dorsocervical fat pad (buffalo hump) and rounded moon facies, proximal myopathy, violaceous wide cutaneous striae exceeding one centimetre on the abdomen, easy bruising, systemic arterial hypertension, and secondary diabetes mellitus.

steps.tx: Autonomous hypersecretion of adrenocorticotropic hormone by a benign pituitary corticotroph microadenoma represents the single most common cause of endogenous hypercortisolism. Designated specifically as **cushing disease**, it accounts for roughly seventy percent of all endogenous cases, predominating in women in their reproductive years. In contrast, ectopic ACTH secretion arises from non-pituitary neuroendocrine malignancies, most frequently small cell lung carcinoma or bronchial carcinoids. Ectopic cases present acutely with severe hyperpigmentation, profound hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, and muscle wasting, often lacking classical centripetal fat accumulation.

left.title: Cushing Disease (Pituitary)
points: Slow, progressive onset of centripetal obesity

right.title: Ectopic ACTH Secretion
points: Small cell lung cancer, bronchial carcinoid tumours
Rapid onset of severe muscle wasting and cachexia

steps.tx: Establishing the biochemical diagnosis of hypercortisolism requires demonstrating the loss of normal circadian glucocorticoid variation or failure of feedback suppression. The overnight one-milligram **dexamethasone suppression test** represents a highly sensitive initial screening tool; failing to suppress morning serum cortisol below one point eight micrograms per decilitre confirms pathological autonomous cortisol synthesis. Alternatively, measuring late-night salivary cortisol across two consecutive evenings reliably detects the loss of the physiological midnight cortisol nadir, offering exceptional sensitivity and non-invasive outpatient convenience.

nodes.label: First-line screening: 1 mg DST (< 1.8 mcg/dL) OR Late-night salivary cortisol
At least two positive first-line screening tests confirm hypercortisolism

steps.tx: Quantifying non-protein-bound circulating glucocorticoid excretion across a complete diurnal cycle corroborates hypercortisolism without venipuncture stress. Measuring **24-hour urinary free cortisol** (UFC) provides an integrated index of daily unbound cortisol filtration by the glomeruli. Urinary values exceeding three times the upper limit of normal unequivocally establish Cushing syndrome. Concurrently, clinicians must exclude pseudo-Cushing states, wherein severe depression, chronic alcohol use disorder, morbid obesity, or severe physiological stress transiently activate the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis without true autonomous neoplastic secretion.

left.title: True Cushing Syndrome
points: Progressive clinical striae, myopathy, and osteopenia

right.title: Pseudo-Cushing States
points: Severe major depression, alcohol dependence, obesity
Preserved diurnal rhythm or suppresses with CRH testing
Resolves fully upon treating the underlying psychiatric condition

steps.tx: Once hypercortisolism is definitively confirmed, measuring plasma adrenocorticotropic hormone bifurcates the diagnostic algorithm into ACTH-dependent and ACTH-independent categories. Undetectable or low ACTH below five picograms per millilitre confirms an ACTH-independent adrenal origin, mandating non-contrast adrenal computed tomography to identify an **adrenal adenoma** or adrenocortical carcinoma. Conversely, normal or elevated ACTH confirms an ACTH-dependent etiology. Differentiating pituitary Cushing disease from ectopic ACTH utilizes high-dose dexamethasone suppression testing and corticotropin-releasing hormone stimulation, followed by bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling if pituitary imaging is equivocal.

steps.tx: Performing **transsphenoidal selective adenomectomy** constitutes the primary curative intervention for pituitary-dependent Cushing disease. Successful surgical excision achieves immediate remission in eighty percent of microadenomas, inducing transient postoperative corticotroph suppression that requires temporary oral hydrocortisone replacement until the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis recovers over six to twelve months. For inoperable cases or refractory hypercortisolism awaiting radiotherapy, steroidogenesis inhibitors including ketoconazole and metyrapone block adrenal enzymatic cortisol synthesis, rapidly normalizing circulating glucocorticoids.

nodes.label: Pituitary Cushing disease confirmed on MRI / IPSS
Post-op morning cortisol < 2 mcg/dL confirms cure (Start hydrocortisone)
Refractory / Recurrent: Medical block (Osilodrostat) OR Bilateral adrenalectomy

steps.tx: Primary adrenocortical insufficiency driven by autoimmune destruction of all three adrenal cortical zones presents as the clinical antithesis of Cushing syndrome. Historically designated as **addison disease**, autoimmune adrenalitis accounts for eighty percent of primary adrenal failure in developed countries, mediated by autoantibodies against 21-hydroxylase. Patients develop severe fatigue, anorexia, unintended weight loss, orthostatic hypotension, and diffuse cutaneous and mucosal hyperpigmentation. Hyperpigmentation arises because deficient cortisol feedback stimulates pro-opiomelanocortin cleavage into ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone, depositing melanin in palmar creases, buccal mucosa, and surgical scars.

left.title: Cushing Syndrome
points: Centripetal obesity, moon facies, buffalo hump
Proximal muscle weakness and skin thinning

right.title: Addison Disease
points: Severe anorexia, weight loss, and postural hypotension
Hyperpigmentation of buccal mucosa and skin creases

steps.tx: Laboratory evaluation of primary adrenal insufficiency exposes concurrent mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid deficiencies. Unlike secondary pituitary adrenal failure where aldosterone secretion is preserved by the renin-angiotensin system, Addison disease destroys the zona glomerulosa. Laboratory profiling characteristically reveals hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, non-anion gap metabolic acidosis, and prerenal azotemia. Baseline diagnostic confirmation requires demonstrating low morning serum cortisol paired with elevated plasma ACTH, prompting immediate physiological **adrenal replacement** with oral hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone.
